entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: The Founding of the Roman Republic
entries.dek: Of how the Romans drove out their last king, and what they built in his place.

pair.left: Livy and Dionysius tell of Lucretia's oath, of Brutus feigning dullness, and of a father who watched his own sons die for treason.
pair.right: Historians suspect the date runs years off, and some, like Cornell, think Porsenna of Clusium briefly held Rome itself.

witnesses: Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities, IV–V

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: Confucius and the Search for a Virtuous Ruler
entries.dek: As the Zhou order fractured, a teacher from Lu sought to restore political authority through ritual, moral cultivation, and the example of the gentleman.
entries.location: State of Lu, Eastern Zhou China

pair.left: The Zuo Commentary and Sima Qian place Confucius in office in Lu, then on long travels through Wei, Song, Chen and Cai in search of a ruler who would govern by the Way.
pair.right: The Analects was compiled across generations; manuscripts from about 300 BC show his sayings circulated early, without proving each one is his.

witnesses: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian

sources.title: New Manuscript Evidence on the Formation of the Analects: The Warring States Anhui University Zhongni Said and the Wangjiazui Kongzi Said

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: From Miletus to Alexandria: Greek Philosophy
entries.dek: Of how Greek philosophy began in free trading cities, survived Athens's death sentence on Socrates, and found its safest home on a king's payroll.

pair.left: Reason freed itself from myth and grew by the force of its own arguments.
pair.right: Philosophy grew where patrons protected it. Cities tolerated it until it touched their politics; kings paid for it when it served their prestige.

witnesses: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: Caesar Crosses the Rubicon
entries.dek: A river, an army, and a decision that turned Rome toward civil war.
entries.location: The Rubicon, between Cisalpine Gaul and Italy

pair.left: Suetonius tells of a night march, a lost road, a piper who seized a trumpet and crossed first, and Caesar's words, "The die is now cast."
pair.right: Neither the exact date nor the river's location is certain; scholars place the crossing on the night of 10–11 January, and Caesar's men had crossed the day before.

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: How a Jewish Sect Became Rome's Religion
entries.dek: Of how the empire that crucified a Galilean preacher ended, 350 years later, by making his church its only lawful faith.

pair.left: The faith spread by the witness of martyrs, and God gave Constantine a sign of victory in the cross.
pair.right: The church grew into an organized network that persecution could not break, and emperors in civil wars found it worth winning.

witnesses: The Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles
Lactantius, On the Deaths of the Persecutors
Eusebius of Caesarea, Life of Constantine

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: Mani and the Making of Manichaeism
entries.dek: Of how a boy raised in a Jewish-Christian baptist sect in Mesopotamia built a world religion from Christian, Buddhist and Zoroastrian parts, and presented it to a Persian king.

pair.left: Mani was the last of the apostles of light, sent after Zoroaster, the Buddha and Jesus to restore the truth their followers had corrupted.
pair.right: Mani grew up among the Elcesaites, broke with them, borrowed from Christian, Buddhist and Zoroastrian teaching, and framed his faith for the Sasanian court.

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: Rise of Islam, 610–750
entries.dek: Of how a prophet's community in Arabia became a state, defeated two empires, and fought itself over who should rule.

pair.left: God revealed the Qur'an to Muhammad, and the community he founded spread the faith from Spain to Central Asia within a century.
pair.right: The early record comes mostly from Muslim histories written generations later. They agree on the outline and differ, often by party, on the succession.

witnesses: Ibn Ishaq, Life of the Messenger of God (as edited by Ibn Hisham)
Al-Tabari, History of the Prophets and Kings

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: Papacy Versus Empire
entries.dek: Of how popes and emperors made each other, then fought for three centuries over who stood higher, and how kings won.

pair.left: Popes claimed that Christ gave Peter's heirs authority over kings; emperors claimed their crown came from God directly, not through Rome.
pair.right: Both claims were weapons in fights over land, revenue and the right to appoint bishops. The winners were the national monarchies that neither side controlled.

witnesses: Dictatus papae, in the register of Gregory VII (1075)
Decree Haec sancta of the Council of Constance (1415)

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: How Buddhism Spread
entries.dek: Of how a wandering teacher's order crossed Asia by winning kings and merchants, and why it grew rich enough for an emperor to seize.

pair.left: The truth of the Dharma persuaded kings and peoples wherever it was preached.
pair.right: Buddhism traveled with royal patrons and trade. Patronage made the monasteries rich, and wealth made them a target.

witnesses: Edicts of Ashoka, Rock Edict XIII

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: The Mongol Empire
entries.dek: Of how a steppe confederation built the largest land empire yet seen, and broke apart over the rule that made it.

pair.left: Chroniclers from Baghdad to Hungary describe the Mongols as a scourge sent to punish sin, sparing no one.
pair.right: The killing was real and vast. So were the trade, the post roads and the movement of people and ideas across one jurisdiction. Both came from the same machine.

witnesses: The Secret History of the Mongols
Gabriel de Mussis, account of the siege of Caffa

sources.title: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
Mongol conquest of the Jin dynasty

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: How France Wrote Women Out of the Crown
entries.dek: Of how two regents took the throne over a king's daughter and a king's grandson, and how a Frankish land code was found later to justify it.

pair.left: An ancient law of the Franks barred women from the French crown and from passing it on, and every king since Clovis had obeyed it.
pair.right: The rule was made in 1317 and 1328 by assemblies backing the strongest claimant. The Salic code was first cited for it around 1358.

witnesses: Declaration of the assembly of February 1317, "Women do not succeed in the kingdom of France"

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: The Long Fall of Constantinople
entries.dek: Of how the city that held for a thousand years was first emptied by its friends, and only then taken by its enemy.

pair.left: The city fell to a great sultan and a great cannon on 29 May 1453, after a heroic last stand.
pair.right: By 1453 the empire had lost its army, its provinces and its money over four centuries. The siege finished a state that could no longer pay for its own defense.

witnesses: Geoffrey of Villehardouin, The Conquest of Constantinople

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: Erasmus and the Reformers
entries.dek: Of how a Catholic scholar's rushed Greek New Testament became the working text of the men who broke with Rome, and why he refused to follow them.

pair.left: Erasmus laid the egg and Luther hatched it. The humanist's mockery of the Church made the Reformation.
pair.right: Erasmus supplied the Reformers' text, their Greek and their method. They drew conclusions he rejected, and he stayed in the Roman Church.

witnesses: Erasmus, Novum Instrumentum omne (Basel, 1516), dedication to Leo X

sources.title: De libero arbitrio diatribe sive collatio

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: The Reformation and Its Wars
entries.dek: Of how a friar's protest became a princes' settlement, and why it took 131 years and a continental war to finish.

pair.left: A lone monk read Scripture, found the Church in error, and the truth he printed set Europe free.
pair.right: The protest survived because printers sold it and princes protected it. Princes, not theologians, drew the final confessional map.

witnesses: Martin Luther, Against the Murderous, Thieving Hordes of Peasants (1525)
The Treaties of Münster and Osnabrück (1648)

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: Merchant Republics to Amsterdam and London
entries.dek: Of how the center of European trade and credit moved north, from Venice and Genoa to Antwerp, Amsterdam and London, carried by wars, defaults and refugees.

pair.left: Thrift, enterprise and good government made each city rich in turn.
pair.right: Each city rose by financing a stronger power's wars and fell when that power defaulted, conquered it, or found a better lender. Capital moved with people fleeing war.

witnesses: Chrysobull of Alexios I for Venice (1082)
Account books of the Peruzzi company (1335–1343)
Charter of the Dutch East India Company (1602)

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: An Assembly Elects the First Romanov
entries.dek: Of how a land without a tsar called an assembly into a burned capital, passed over foreign princes and great boyars, and chose a sixteen-year-old.

pair.left: The whole land, moved by God, chose with one voice the nearest kin of the old dynasty, and peace returned with him.
pair.right: Boyars, Cossacks and town delegates bargained for weeks. Michael won as the candidate who threatened the fewest factions, and his father ruled.

witnesses: Charter of the Election of Michael Romanov (1613)

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: Money and Central Banking
entries.dek: Of how money passed from stamped metal to a government's promise, and how lenders and rulers built the banks that keep it.

pair.left: Sound institutions, built by prudent men, gave nations stable money and cheap credit.
pair.right: Each new institution was a deal between a ruler who needed to borrow and lenders who wanted security. When the deal broke, the money did too.

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: The Treaty of Madrid and the Guaraní War
entries.dek: Of how two crowns redrew South America on a map, traded seven Jesuit missions for a smuggling port, and sent armies when the Guaraní refused to leave.

pair.left: Each side should keep what it held, along rivers and mountains, and the old papal line was dead letter. A clean border would bring peace.
pair.right: Portugal wanted the gold country and the mission lands; Spain wanted Colonia closed to smugglers. The people on the ceded land were not asked.

witnesses: Treaty of Madrid, 13 January 1750 (preamble and 26 articles)
Alexandre de Gusmão, Mapa das Cortes (1749)

sources.title: Suppression of the Society of Jesus

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: The Age of Revolutions
entries.dek: Of how the cost of winning wars broke three empires, and how revolution passed from Boston to Paris to Saint-Domingue to Caracas.

pair.left: Free peoples rose against tyranny in the name of the rights of man, and each revolution inspired the next.
pair.right: Each revolution began in a fiscal or dynastic crisis of the empire above it. Ideas spread fast, but war debt and empty thrones opened the door.

witnesses: The Stamp Act (1765) and the resolutions of the Stamp Act Congress

sources.title: France in the American Revolutionary War

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: Spinoza to Hegel: The Pantheism Controversy
entries.dek: Of how a dramatist's private confession, published by a merchant's son to discredit reason, put a banned philosopher at the center of German thought.

pair.left: Spinoza was the necessary starting point of modern philosophy, and German thought rose by absorbing and surpassing him.
pair.right: Spinoza re-entered German debate through a quarrel over a dead man's reputation. Jacobi publicized him as a warning, and a generation read him as a revelation.

witnesses: Friedrich Heinrich Jacobi, Über die Lehre des Spinoza in Briefen an Herrn Moses Mendelssohn (1785)
G. W. F. Hegel, Phenomenology of Spirit, Preface (1807)
G. W. F. Hegel, Lectures on the History of Philosophy, "Spinoza"

sources.title: Lectures on the History of Philosophy: Spinoza

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: Opium, Trade and the Qing
entries.dek: Of how Britain paid for its tea with Indian opium, went to war to keep selling it, and opened China to a century of foreign power.

pair.left: British officials spoke of free trade and equal diplomacy; Qing officials spoke of a poison smuggled in by barbarians who would not obey the law.
pair.right: Both sides were defending money. Britain needed opium to pay for tea; the Qing needed silver and authority. Force decided the question, and the Qing paid the bill for sixty years.

witnesses: Qianlong Emperor, edict to George III (1793)
Lin Zexu, letter to Queen Victoria (1839)

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: The Russian Revolution
entries.dek: Of how the Bolsheviks took the capital, and turned the state against the Church.

pair.left: The Church counts its martyrs by the thousand, from the executions of the civil war to the purges of 1937–38.
pair.right: The persecution is not in doubt; its toll is. Counts of clergy killed run from about 1,200 to more than 100,000, depending on years and sources.

witnesses: John Reed, Ten Days That Shook the World (1919)
Lenin's secret letter on the seizure of church valuables (1922)

sources.title: Persecution of Christians in the Soviet Union

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: 1918: The Great War Ends
entries.dek: Of how four years of industrial war ended in a railway carriage, and what the peace that followed left to the century.

pair.left: Soldiers on the line remembered the last morning as silence and exhaustion, Germans bowing as they withdrew, shelling that went on to dusk.
pair.right: The dead are counted in ranges, not totals; civilian and pandemic figures in particular vary by millions between estimates.

witnesses: British and American soldiers' accounts of 11 November 1918
Marshal Ferdinand Foch, on the Treaty of Versailles

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: How Wicca Was Assembled
entries.dek: Of how an Egyptologist's theory, a London magical order, a ceremonial magician's rituals and a retired colonial officer's Masonic habits became a new English religion.

pair.left: A hidden coven in the New Forest had kept the old pagan witch religion alive for centuries, and it let one initiate reveal it.
pair.right: The coven most likely formed in the 1930s from Murray's theory. Gardner and his priestesses built the rites from ceremonial magic, Crowley and Freemasonry.

witnesses: Margaret Murray, The Witch-Cult in Western Europe (1921)

sources.title: Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn
Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: Decolonization
entries.dek: Of how Europe's empires divided Africa and Asia, armed their subjects with the language of self-determination, and lost them within two generations.

pair.left: Peoples long held in subjection rose and took back their freedom.
pair.right: Nationalist movements won, but they won against powers that two world wars had weakened, bankrupted and placed under American and Soviet pressure. The timing came from Europe's exhaustion.

witnesses: General Act of the Berlin Conference (1885)
Nguyễn Ái Quốc and others, petition to the Versailles conference (1919)

sources.title: Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples

entries.author: ΛRX Atlas
entries.title: Second Vatican Council
entries.dek: Of how an old pope called the bishops of the world to Rome, and what they changed.

pair.left: John XXIII spoke of aggiornamento, bringing the Church up to date, and asked for "the medicine of mercy" rather than condemnation.
pair.right: Benedict XVI read the council as reform within continuity; traditionalists hold three of its texts break with earlier teaching.

witnesses: John XXIII, Gaudet Mater Ecclesia (opening address, 11 October 1962)
Benedict XVI, address to the Roman Curia (22 December 2005)

sources.title: John XXIII and the open window
Religion News Service on John XXIII
